## Lantana Reinvasion at EBTL: Where, When, and How to Schedule Follow-Up

### Site context

EBTL is ~70 acres of degraded dry deciduous forest in the Eastern Ghats foothills near Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu (South Deccan plateau). The climate is seasonal with a pronounced monsoon. This places it squarely in the ecosystem type studied by Prasad et al. (2018), Ramaswami & Sukumar (2013), and Sundaram et al. (2018) in similar South Indian dry deciduous forests.

---

### 1. Where will it come back first?

In order of priority for surveillance:

| Priority | Zone | Why |
|----------|------|-----|
| **1** | **Stream/water-body edges and drainage lines** | Lantana stem abundance and thicket area are highest closest to streams across South Indian landscapes (Ramaswami & Sukumar, 2014, *J. Biosciences* 39:717-726, Mudumalai study). Water disperses seeds and provides moisture for establishment. EBTL has a lake and likely seasonal drainage — these are your hotspots. |
| **2** | **Boundaries adjoining uncleared Lantana** | Seed rain from adjacent uncleared stands is a primary recolonisation vector (Babu et al., 2009; study at Rajaji NP in *Indian Forester*). Any edge of your 70 acres that borders untreated forest or scrub will receive bird-dispersed and wind-blown seed continuously. |
| **3** | **Disturbed/bare soil from the clearing operation itself** | Mechanical removal exposes buried seeds to light, which is the primary germination trigger for Lantana (Love et al., 2009, Corbett TR study). Areas where heavy uprooting occurred — especially dense thicket zones — will have the most soil disturbance and the richest seed bank. Seeds can constitute 50-70% of the total soil seed bank under former dense stands (Babu et al., 2009, *IJERT*). |
| **4** | **Open/unshaded areas and canopy gaps** | Lantana does not invade intact canopy; it exploits gaps (Gentle & Duggin, 1997; GISD profile). Any part of the site where native canopy has not yet closed will be vulnerable. |

**Bottom line for EBTL specifically:** Walk the lake shore, drainage lines, and the perimeter fence-line adjacent to uncleared hillside first. These will show regrowth before interior areas do.

---

### 2. How quickly does it come back?

The research is consistent across multiple South Indian studies:

| Event | Timeline | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **Seed germination flush** | During and immediately after the monsoon (Jun-Sep in Tamil Nadu). Seedlings appear within 2-4 weeks of sustained rain on exposed soil. | Phenology study, *Plant Science Today* (Jeevanandam et al.); Prasad et al. 2018 |
| **Visible seedling carpet** | 3-6 months post-clearing, concentrated after the first monsoon. | Rufford project interim report (BRT, Karnataka): understory monitoring at 6-month intervals post-removal showed Lantana seedlings present at the first check. |
| **Rootstock resprouting** (if roots were left) | Within weeks of cutting. Stumps resprout vigorously unless the root crown is removed to 3-5 cm below soil. | ARC-PPRI leaflet; Babu et al. 2009 |
| **Dense thicket re-establishment** (if no follow-up) | 1-2 growing seasons (~12-18 months). Sites cleared only once at Rajaji NP were "rapidly recolonized" within this window. | Babu et al., *Indian Forester*; Hiremath et al. 2018 |
| **Seed bank exhaustion** (with repeated weeding) | 2-4 years of consistent follow-up. Seeds remain viable >1 year in soil; the CAMPA proposal notes "viability of more than one year." | Singh & Angiras 2011; CAMPA 2022 proposal; Tireman 1916 (historical confirmation) |

---

### 3. Recommended follow-up schedule for EBTL

Based on the above, here is a practical calendar. I'm assuming initial clearing happens in the dry season (Nov-Mar), which is standard practice (CAMPA proposal recommends "non-flowering season i.e. winter season"):

| When | Action | Focus zones |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **Oct-Nov (end of first monsoon)** | First follow-up weeding. This is the single most important intervention. Pull/uproot all Lantana seedlings while the ground is still soft. | Entire cleared area, prioritising stream edges and perimeter |
| **Feb-Mar (dry season, Year 1)** | Second weeding pass. Catch any rootstock resprouts and late germinants. Also remove secondary invaders (*Chromolaena*, *Parthenium*). | Heavily disturbed soil zones, gaps |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 2)** | Third weeding. Seed bank begins depleting but is not exhausted. | Edges, drainage, any spots missed previously |
| **Feb-Mar (Year 2)** | Fourth weeding. Assess whether native grass/forb cover is suppressing Lantana recruitment. Where it isn't, consider sowing native grass seed. | Open/bare patches |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 3)** | Fifth weeding. By now, with consistent effort, Lantana density should be very low. | Spot checks, perimeter patrol |
| **Annually thereafter** | Monitoring walk, especially perimeter and watercourses. Weed opportunistically. | Perimeter + riparian zones |

**Minimum commitment: 4 weeding rounds over 2 years.** Prasad et al. (2018) found that "uprooting combined with weeding of germinating Lantana, particularly after the rainy season, minimized overall re-invasion." The Himachal Pradesh data (Singh & Angiras, 2011) showed that 4-6 cuttings at 45-day intervals can exhaust root nutrient reserves entirely.

---

### 4. Key variables that affect your specific timeline

- **Rainfall.** EBTL/Krishnagiri receives ~800-900 mm annually (relatively dry for Tamil Nadu). Prasad et al. (2018) found drier sites have *lower* reinvasion rates — this works in your favour. Expect less aggressive regrowth than wetter sites like Mudumalai or BRT.
- **Native cover recovery.** The faster native grasses and forbs establish, the more they shade out Lantana seedlings (which need light to germinate). Active seeding of native species accelerates this (CAMPA proposal; Bolosha, 2024).
- **Proximity to source populations.** If the surrounding hills still harbour dense Lantana, bird-dispersed seed will keep arriving indefinitely. Perimeter vigilance is permanent.

<content>Since its introduction in India 200 years ago, Lantana camara (Lantana) has become established and naturalised across a wide range of habitats. In Indian protected areas, lantana has been predominately managed using a range of mechanical removal approaches, costing up to 6000 per hectare. However, managed sites are rapidly recolonized by lantana and management programmes rarely achieve their goal of lantana eradication. In present study, we quantified recolonisation of lantana at sites that were either managed only once or for two consecutive years in Rajaji National Park, Uttarakhand. Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

Synthesis:
Lantana camara is a highly resilient invasive shrub that rapidly recolonizes cleared areas in India through rootstock regeneration and a persistent soil seed bank [1][2]. Because the species typically germinates during the monsoon season (June to September), seedling regrowth is most active during and immediately following these months [3][4][5]. Successful management requires continuous, multi-year intervention, as studies indicate that eradication is rarely achieved with a single removal effort [1][6]. Now I have enough research to provide a thorough, evidence-based answer. Here it is:

---

## Lantana Reinvasion at EBTL: Where, When, and How to Schedule Follow-Up

### Site context

EBTL is ~70 acres of degraded dry deciduous forest in the Eastern Ghats foothills near Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu (South Deccan plateau). The climate is seasonal with a pronounced monsoon. This places it squarely in the ecosystem type studied by Prasad et al. (2018), Ramaswami & Sukumar (2013), and Sundaram et al. (2018) in similar South Indian dry deciduous forests.

---

### 1. Where will it come back first?

In order of priority for surveillance:

| Priority | Zone | Why |
|----------|------|-----|
| **1** | **Stream/water-body edges and drainage lines** | Lantana stem abundance and thicket area are highest closest to streams across South Indian landscapes (Ramaswami & Sukumar, 2014, *J. Biosciences* 39:717-726, Mudumalai study). Water disperses seeds and provides moisture for establishment. EBTL has a lake and likely seasonal drainage — these are your hotspots. |
| **2** | **Boundaries adjoining uncleared Lantana** | Seed rain from adjacent uncleared stands is a primary recolonisation vector (Babu et al., 2009; study at Rajaji NP in *Indian Forester*). Any edge of your 70 acres that borders untreated forest or scrub will receive bird-dispersed and wind-blown seed continuously. |
| **3** | **Disturbed/bare soil from the clearing operation itself** | Mechanical removal exposes buried seeds to light, which is the primary germination trigger for Lantana (Love et al., 2009, Corbett TR study). Areas where heavy uprooting occurred — especially dense thicket zones — will have the most soil disturbance and the richest seed bank. Seeds can constitute 50-70% of the total soil seed bank under former dense stands (Babu et al., 2009, *IJERT*). |
| **4** | **Open/unshaded areas and canopy gaps** | Lantana does not invade intact canopy; it exploits gaps (Gentle & Duggin, 1997; GISD profile). Any part of the site where native canopy has not yet closed will be vulnerable. |

**Bottom line for EBTL specifically:** Walk the lake shore, drainage lines, and the perimeter fence-line adjacent to uncleared hillside first. These will show regrowth before interior areas do.

---

### 2. How quickly does it come back?

The research is consistent across multiple South Indian studies:

| Event | Timeline | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **Seed germination flush** | During and immediately after the monsoon (Jun-Sep in Tamil Nadu). Seedlings appear within 2-4 weeks of sustained rain on exposed soil. | Phenology study, *Plant Science Today* (Jeevanandam et al.); Prasad et al. 2018 |
| **Visible seedling carpet** | 3-6 months post-clearing, concentrated after the first monsoon. | Rufford project interim report (BRT, Karnataka): understory monitoring at 6-month intervals post-removal showed Lantana seedlings present at the first check. |
| **Rootstock resprouting** (if roots were left) | Within weeks of cutting. Stumps resprout vigorously unless the root crown is removed to 3-5 cm below soil. | ARC-PPRI leaflet; Babu et al. 2009 |
| **Dense thicket re-establishment** (if no follow-up) | 1-2 growing seasons (~12-18 months). Sites cleared only once at Rajaji NP were "rapidly recolonized" within this window. | Babu et al., *Indian Forester*; Hiremath et al. 2018 |
| **Seed bank exhaustion** (with repeated weeding) | 2-4 years of consistent follow-up. Seeds remain viable >1 year in soil; the CAMPA proposal notes "viability of more than one year." | Singh & Angiras 2011; CAMPA 2022 proposal; Tireman 1916 (historical confirmation) |

---

### 3. Recommended follow-up schedule for EBTL

Based on the above, here is a practical calendar. I'm assuming initial clearing happens in the dry season (Nov-Mar), which is standard practice (CAMPA proposal recommends "non-flowering season i.e. winter season"):

| When | Action | Focus zones |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **Oct-Nov (end of first monsoon)** | First follow-up weeding. This is the single most important intervention. Pull/uproot all Lantana seedlings while the ground is still soft. | Entire cleared area, prioritising stream edges and perimeter |
| **Feb-Mar (dry season, Year 1)** | Second weeding pass. Catch any rootstock resprouts and late germinants. Also remove secondary invaders (*Chromolaena*, *Parthenium*). | Heavily disturbed soil zones, gaps |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 2)** | Third weeding. Seed bank begins depleting but is not exhausted. | Edges, drainage, any spots missed previously |
| **Feb-Mar (Year 2)** | Fourth weeding. Assess whether native grass/forb cover is suppressing Lantana recruitment. Where it isn't, consider sowing native grass seed. | Open/bare patches |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 3)** | Fifth weeding. By now, with consistent effort, Lantana density should be very low. | Spot checks, perimeter patrol |
| **Annually thereafter** | Monitoring walk, especially perimeter and watercourses. Weed opportunistically. | Perimeter + riparian zones |

**Minimum commitment: 4 weeding rounds over 2 years.** Prasad et al. (2018) found that "uprooting combined with weeding of germinating Lantana, particularly after the rainy season, minimized overall re-invasion." The Himachal Pradesh data (Singh & Angiras, 2011) showed that 4-6 cuttings at 45-day intervals can exhaust root nutrient reserves entirely.

---

### 4. Key variables that affect your specific timeline

- **Rainfall.** EBTL/Krishnagiri receives ~800-900 mm annually (relatively dry for Tamil Nadu). Prasad et al. (2018) found drier sites have *lower* reinvasion rates — this works in your favour. Expect less aggressive regrowth than wetter sites like Mudumalai or BRT.
- **Native cover recovery.** The faster native grasses and forbs establish, the more they shade out Lantana seedlings (which need light to germinate). Active seeding of native species accelerates this (CAMPA proposal; Bolosha, 2024).
- **Proximity to source populations.** If the surrounding hills still harbour dense Lantana, bird-dispersed seed will keep arriving indefinitely. Perimeter vigilance is permanent.

---

## Lantana Reinvasion at EBTL: Where, When, and How to Schedule Follow-Up

### Site context

EBTL is ~70 acres of degraded dry deciduous forest in the Eastern Ghats foothills near Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu (South Deccan plateau). The climate is seasonal with a pronounced monsoon. This places it squarely in the ecosystem type studied by Prasad et al. (2018), Ramaswami & Sukumar (2013), and Sundaram et al. (2018) in similar South Indian dry deciduous forests.

---

### 1. Where will it come back first?

In order of priority for surveillance:

| Priority | Zone | Why |
|----------|------|-----|
| **1** | **Stream/water-body edges and drainage lines** | Lantana stem abundance and thicket area are highest closest to streams across South Indian landscapes (Ramaswami & Sukumar, 2014, *J. Biosciences* 39:717-726, Mudumalai study). Water disperses seeds and provides moisture for establishment. EBTL has a lake and likely seasonal drainage — these are your hotspots. |
| **2** | **Boundaries adjoining uncleared Lantana** | Seed rain from adjacent uncleared stands is a primary recolonisation vector (Babu et al., 2009; study at Rajaji NP in *Indian Forester*). Any edge of your 70 acres that borders untreated forest or scrub will receive bird-dispersed and wind-blown seed continuously. |
| **3** | **Disturbed/bare soil from the clearing operation itself** | Mechanical removal exposes buried seeds to light, which is the primary germination trigger for Lantana (Love et al., 2009, Corbett TR study). Areas where heavy uprooting occurred — especially dense thicket zones — will have the most soil disturbance and the richest seed bank. Seeds can constitute 50-70% of the total soil seed bank under former dense stands (Babu et al., 2009, *IJERT*). |
| **4** | **Open/unshaded areas and canopy gaps** | Lantana does not invade intact canopy; it exploits gaps (Gentle & Duggin, 1997; GISD profile). Any part of the site where native canopy has not yet closed will be vulnerable. |

**Bottom line for EBTL specifically:** Walk the lake shore, drainage lines, and the perimeter fence-line adjacent to uncleared hillside first. These will show regrowth before interior areas do.

---

### 2. How quickly does it come back?

The research is consistent across multiple South Indian studies:

| Event | Timeline | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **Seed germination flush** | During and immediately after the monsoon (Jun-Sep in Tamil Nadu). Seedlings appear within 2-4 weeks of sustained rain on exposed soil. | Phenology study, *Plant Science Today* (Jeevanandam et al.); Prasad et al. 2018 |
| **Visible seedling carpet** | 3-6 months post-clearing, concentrated after the first monsoon. | Rufford project interim report (BRT, Karnataka): understory monitoring at 6-month intervals post-removal showed Lantana seedlings present at the first check. |
| **Rootstock resprouting** (if roots were left) | Within weeks of cutting. Stumps resprout vigorously unless the root crown is removed to 3-5 cm below soil. | ARC-PPRI leaflet; Babu et al. 2009 |
| **Dense thicket re-establishment** (if no follow-up) | 1-2 growing seasons (~12-18 months). Sites cleared only once at Rajaji NP were "rapidly recolonized" within this window. | Babu et al., *Indian Forester*; Hiremath et al. 2018 |
| **Seed bank exhaustion** (with repeated weeding) | 2-4 years of consistent follow-up. Seeds remain viable >1 year in soil; the CAMPA proposal notes "viability of more than one year." | Singh & Angiras 2011; CAMPA 2022 proposal; Tireman 1916 (historical confirmation) |

---

### 3. Recommended follow-up schedule for EBTL

Based on the above, here is a practical calendar. I'm assuming initial clearing happens in the dry season (Nov-Mar), which is standard practice (CAMPA proposal recommends "non-flowering season i.e. winter season"):

| When | Action | Focus zones |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **Oct-Nov (end of first monsoon)** | First follow-up weeding. This is the single most important intervention. Pull/uproot all Lantana seedlings while the ground is still soft. | Entire cleared area, prioritising stream edges and perimeter |
| **Feb-Mar (dry season, Year 1)** | Second weeding pass. Catch any rootstock resprouts and late germinants. Also remove secondary invaders (*Chromolaena*, *Parthenium*). | Heavily disturbed soil zones, gaps |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 2)** | Third weeding. Seed bank begins depleting but is not exhausted. | Edges, drainage, any spots missed previously |
| **Feb-Mar (Year 2)** | Fourth weeding. Assess whether native grass/forb cover is suppressing Lantana recruitment. Where it isn't, consider sowing native grass seed. | Open/bare patches |
| **Oct-Nov (Year 3)** | Fifth weeding. By now, with consistent effort, Lantana density should be very low. | Spot checks, perimeter patrol |
| **Annually thereafter** | Monitoring walk, especially perimeter and watercourses. Weed opportunistically. | Perimeter + riparian zones |

**Minimum commitment: 4 weeding rounds over 2 years.** Prasad et al. (2018) found that "uprooting combined with weeding of germinating Lantana, particularly after the rainy season, minimized overall re-invasion." The Himachal Pradesh data (Singh & Angiras, 2011) showed that 4-6 cuttings at 45-day intervals can exhaust root nutrient reserves entirely.

---

### 4. Key variables that affect your specific timeline

- **Rainfall.** EBTL/Krishnagiri receives ~800-900 mm annually (relatively dry for Tamil Nadu). Prasad et al. (2018) found drier sites have *lower* reinvasion rates — this works in your favour. Expect less aggressive regrowth than wetter sites like Mudumalai or BRT.
- **Native cover recovery.** The faster native grasses and forbs establish, the more they shade out Lantana seedlings (which need light to germinate). Active seeding of native species accelerates this (CAMPA proposal; Bolosha, 2024).
- **Proximity to source populations.** If the surrounding hills still harbour dense Lantana, bird-dispersed seed will keep arriving indefinitely. Perimeter vigilance is permanent.
